lessons.t: What a main claim actually is
lessons.intro: You will learn what a main claim is and how it differs from the topic of a text. Finding it is the first step to judging any argument fairly.

cards.b: The topic is what a text is about, such as city parking. The claim is what the writer wants you to accept about that topic, such as that parking charges should rise. A text can cover a topic without making any claim at all.

A real claim takes a side that someone could disagree with. The sky is blue is a fact, while parking charges should rise can be argued either way. Good readers look for the claim that could reasonably be challenged.

Try to restate the whole passage as one sentence that begins with the writer's point. If you cannot, you may be reading a list of facts rather than an argument. Use this test on every text you read closely.

fig.title: Finding the main claim
fig.note: Move from subject to the writer's specific point.

ex.q: Which sentence is a claim rather than just a topic?
o: Many bikes are sold each year
Cities should build protected bike lanes
ex.why: The first two options name a subject or report a fact. The third takes a side about what cities should do, so someone could disagree with it, which makes it a claim.

lessons.tip: If you can argue against a sentence, it is probably a claim.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a topic and a claim?
o: A topic is a subject, a claim is a point about it
A claim is always a fact
A topic is always in the title
quiz.why: A topic names what the text is about, while a claim states what the writer wants you to believe about that subject.

quiz.q: Which statement is most clearly a claim?
o: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level
Schools should start later in the morning
quiz.why: Starting later is a position people can dispute, while the other options are facts or descriptions.

lessons.t: Spotting the thesis in an opening
lessons.intro: You will learn where writers usually state their main claim and how to recognise it quickly. This saves time when you read essays, reports and articles.

cards.b: Many essays state the main claim in the first or second paragraph. Writers do this to tell readers what to expect from the rest of the piece. Look there first before reading everything closely.
Words such as however, but and yet often signal a turn toward the writer's real point. A sentence that follows a concession is often the claim. Read those sentences with extra care.
The closing paragraph usually restates the main claim in new words. If the ending says something similar to an early line, you have probably found the thesis. Compare the two to check your reading.

fig.title: Opening versus closing claims
fig.note: Both places often reveal the same main point.

ex.q: An essay's first paragraph says: 'Most cities could cut traffic by building more cycle paths.' What is the main claim?
o: Most cities could cut traffic with cycle paths
ex.why: The first sentence states a position about what cities could do, which is the thesis. The other options mention background topics or details that the sentence does not present as its main point.

lessons.tip: Read the first and last paragraphs before the middle when you are short of time.

quiz.q: Where do writers most often place a thesis?
o: Early in the text, often the first paragraph
quiz.why: Writers usually state the main claim early so readers know what to expect.

quiz.q: Which signal word often introduces a writer's real point?
quiz.why: However turns away from a concession toward the writer's own view, which often holds the claim.

lessons.t: Claims versus facts and opinions
lessons.intro: You will learn to separate facts, opinions and claims in a text. Confusing them is one of the most common reasons readers misjudge an argument.

cards.b: A fact can be confirmed with evidence, such as a measurement, a record or a reliable count. Stating that a city has 1.2 million residents is a fact because a census can confirm it. Facts are not argued about in the same way claims are.

An opinion expresses how someone feels or what they prefer, such as calling a film beautiful. Opinions are personal, so they do not need proof to be sincere. They also rarely carry the weight of an argument on their own.

A claim is a position that a reasonable person could dispute, even if it is supported by facts. Saying that a city should lower its speed limits is a claim, because it asks you to accept a judgement. Writers often use facts to support their claims.

fig.title: Sorting a statement
fig.note: Check each statement in this order.

ex.q: Which statement is a fact rather than a claim or an opinion?
o: The new library is the most beautiful building in town
The library opened in 2019 and holds 40,000 books
Libraries should be funded by taxes
Reading is the best way to relax
ex.why: The second option gives a date and a number that can be checked against records. The other options express taste or take a debatable position, so they are opinions or claims.

lessons.tip: Ask whether a reasonable person could disagree, then whether it can be checked.

quiz.q: What makes a statement a claim?
o: It is a debatable position the writer wants you to accept
It is written in the first person
quiz.why: A claim asks for agreement with a position that could reasonably be disputed.

quiz.q: Which is an opinion?
o: This museum is dull and tiring
quiz.why: Calling the museum dull expresses a personal judgement, while the other options can be verified.

lessons.t: Finding the claim in a news report
lessons.intro: You will learn to find the central claim in a news report, even when it is buried under dramatic details. This helps you tell what a story asserts from what it merely describes.

cards.b: A headline often sums up the most striking claim in a story. It may simplify or exaggerate, so check the body text to see what the reporter actually argues. Treat the headline as a starting point rather than the final answer.

Many news stories open with a person or scene, then move to the wider point. The claim usually appears in the first few paragraphs after that opening. Ask what the story wants you to conclude from the example.

A quoted expert may support the claim, but the reporter's own sentence often states it. Check whether a quote agrees with the reporter or is being used as a counterpoint. Sorting these roles keeps you from confusing them.

fig.title: Average trip times, minutes
fig.note: Shortest average trip in this survey: cycling.

ex.q: A news story says 'Cycling is now the quickest way to cross the city', and the chart shows average trip times of 28 minutes by bike, 35 by car and 42 by bus. Which is the main claim?
o: Cycling is the quickest way to cross the city
ex.why: The quoted sentence states the position the story argues for, and the chart supports it because bikes have the shortest average time. The other options are not the story's claim.

lessons.tip: The sentence that says what should be believed is usually the claim.

quiz.q: Why should you check the body of a news story rather than only the headline?
o: Headlines are always written by experts
Headlines can simplify or exaggerate the point
quiz.why: Headlines are written to attract attention, so they may overstate or simplify what the article argues.

quiz.q: In the story above, what role does the 28-minute average play?
o: It is an opinion about bikes
It is a counterpoint to the claim
It is evidence supporting the claim
quiz.why: The average trip time is a measured figure that supports the claim that cycling is quickest.

lessons.t: Separating the main point from examples
lessons.intro: You will learn to tell the main point of a passage apart from the examples that illustrate it. Mixing them up leads to summaries that focus on the wrong sentence.

cards.b: An example is a specific case that makes a point easier to picture, such as one city that cut traffic. A claim is the broader point that the example is meant to support. If you remove the example, the claim should still stand as a general statement.

Ask whether one sentence is supported by another by placing because between them. If the sentence after because explains the first, the first is probably the claim. The other sentence is the reason or example.

A good summary keeps the main point and drops most of the examples. If your summary includes every detail, you have not yet separated the claim from its support. Try rewriting it in one sentence to check.

fig.title: Claim at the top, support below
fig.note: The highlighted cell is the claim; the rest supports it.

ex.q: Read: 'Libraries matter. In one town, the library runs free job classes that helped 300 people find work last year.' Which sentence is the main claim?
o: In one town, the library runs free job classes
ex.why: Libraries matter states the broad point. The job classes and the 300 people are a specific example that supports it.

lessons.tip: Ask what the example is an example of.

quiz.q: What is the role of a specific example in an argument?
o: To make the claim easier to picture and check
quiz.why: Examples illustrate a general point so readers can see how it applies in practice.

quiz.q: Which sentence is most likely a supporting detail?
o: Fares rose 12 percent in one year
quiz.why: A specific figure about fares supports a broader argument about transport, while the others state positions.

lessons.t: Using signal words to locate claims
lessons.intro: You will learn which signal words tend to introduce a claim and how to use them when skimming. They give you fast clues to where the writer's point is.

cards.b: Words such as therefore, thus, so and consequently often introduce what the writer concludes. A sentence beginning with one of these usually states a claim supported by what came before. Check the preceding sentences to see the reasoning.

Phrases such as the key point is, most importantly, or the real issue often flag a claim directly. Writers use them when they want readers to slow down. Treat the sentence that follows as a likely thesis.

Signal words only suggest a claim, and some sentences contain them without asserting anything. Writers sometimes use so as a casual filler. Always confirm the claim by checking whether the sentence takes a debatable position.

fig.title: Facts lead to the claim
fig.note: Signal words like thus mark the conclusion.

ex.q: Which sentence is most likely to contain the writer's claim?
o: The survey was sent to 500 households
Thus, the council should fund more bus routes
The bus routes run every twenty minutes
ex.why: Thus signals a conclusion drawn from evidence, and should fund takes a debatable position. The other options describe methods or facts.

lessons.tip: A conclusion word often points straight at the claim.

quiz.q: What does the word therefore usually signal?
o: A conclusion drawn from earlier points
quiz.why: Therefore introduces a result that follows from the reasoning before it.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to rely only on signal words?
o: They never appear in real arguments
They are always in the title
Some sentences use them without making a claim
quiz.why: Signal words can be used loosely, so you still need to check whether the sentence asserts a debatable position.

lessons.t: Claims hidden in titles and headlines
lessons.intro: You will learn how titles and headlines can state a claim in a few words. Learning to unpack them helps you judge what an article will argue before you read it.

cards.b: A headline like Remote work boosts output compresses a full argument into a few words. The verb often carries the claim, so look at what it asserts. Unpack the title into a full sentence to see the position it takes.

A title phrased as a question, such as Is homework useful?, often hides a claim that the article answers. Writers may suggest an answer in the first lines. Look for the answer rather than stopping at the question.

Short titles can make a claim sound bigger than the evidence supports, for example by using words like all or always. Check whether the article limits the claim to some cases. Compare the title's strength with the body's.

fig.title: Checking a title's claim
fig.note: Test the headline against what the article actually argues.

ex.q: The headline says 'Coffee prevents illness.' A study found coffee drinkers had slightly fewer colds in one group of 200 adults. Which option states the claim more accurately than the headline?
o: Coffee may be linked to fewer colds in one study
ex.why: The headline overstates by saying coffee prevents illness, which one study cannot show. The accurate version is a hedged link found in one group, while the other options are unrelated or overstated.

lessons.tip: Rewrite the headline as a sentence and check each word for strength.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a headline that says always or never?
o: It may claim more than the evidence supports
quiz.why: Absolute words can make a claim sound stronger than the study or article actually shows.

quiz.q: How should you treat a title phrased as a question?
o: Look for the answer the article gives
Skip to the final page only
quiz.why: A question title often points to a claim, and the article's answer is the claim to identify.

lessons.t: Summarising an argument in one sentence
lessons.intro: You will learn how to compress an argument into a single accurate sentence. A good one-sentence summary shows you have understood the claim and its support.

cards.b: Start by identifying the main claim, then state it in your own words. Avoid copying the first sentence you read. A summary built on the claim will be more accurate than one built on details.
Mention the most important reason or two that support the claim. Leave out vivid examples, dates and quotes, since they are not needed for the core message. Keep the summary to a single sentence.
Compare your summary with the passage to make sure nothing important has changed. A summary that adds a claim the writer did not make is a distortion. Adjust any wording that goes beyond the text.

fig.title: Summary loop
fig.note: Repeat until the sentence matches the text.

ex.q: A passage argues that schools should teach budgeting because students who learn it borrow less later. Which is the best one-sentence summary?
o: Schools should teach budgeting because it reduces later borrowing
Some students are good at maths
ex.why: This sentence states the claim and includes the key reason. The other options are unrelated or reverse the argument.

lessons.tip: A summary should be shorter than the passage but never contradict it.

quiz.q: What should a one-sentence summary include?
o: The main claim and its key reason
quiz.why: A good summary keeps the central claim and its most important support.

quiz.q: A summary says a writer wants fewer cars. The text argues for more cycle lanes. What is wrong?
quiz.why: A summary must match the writer's actual position, and this one changes it.

lessons.t: Qualified claims and hedged language
lessons.intro: You will learn how to read claims that use qualifiers such as may, some and often. Recognising the strength of a claim tells you how far the evidence can take it.

cards.b: Words such as may, might, some and often limit a claim to a degree. A claim that exercise may improve sleep is far weaker than one saying it always does. Read the qualifier carefully, since it defines what the writer is willing to defend.

Phrases like the evidence suggests or appears to be linked signal that the writer is not certain. Hedging is appropriate when data are limited or mixed. A well-hedged claim is often more trustworthy than a confident one with weak support.

Words like proves, guarantees or everyone make big demands on the evidence. If a study of 100 people is used to support a claim about everyone, the claim is overstated. Match the strength of the claim to the strength of the evidence.

fig.title: Test scores by sleep
fig.note: Scores rose with more sleep in this one study.

ex.q: A study of 60 students found those who slept 8 hours scored higher in tests. Which claim is best supported?
o: More sleep may be linked to higher test scores
Everyone should sleep 8 hours to pass
ex.why: The qualified claim matches a single study of 60 students and does not claim certainty. The other options use absolute words that go beyond what the study can show.

lessons.tip: Underline the qualifier, because it defines how far the claim goes.

quiz.q: Which word makes a claim weakest?
quiz.why: Might limits the claim to a possibility, while the other words claim certainty or universality.

quiz.q: Why do careful writers hedge their claims?
o: To match the claim to limited or mixed evidence
quiz.why: Hedging signals that the evidence supports the claim only to a degree.

lessons.t: Tracing a claim across a long essay
lessons.intro: You will learn to follow a single claim through a long essay, from its first statement to its final conclusion. Tracking it keeps you oriented when the text takes detours.

cards.b: In a long essay, each section usually supports, tests or extends the main claim. Ask what role each section plays before you move on. Sections that do none of these may be digressions to note.

Writers often narrow or sharpen their claim as they go, such as moving from all schools to primary schools. Notice when a later statement changes the earlier one. The final version is usually the claim you should report.
Jot one line per section stating how it relates to the claim. This gives you a quick map to review before answering questions. Use the map to check whether the conclusion matches the original claim.

fig.title: Tracking one claim
fig.note: The highlighted cell marks where the claim is first stated.

ex.q: An essay opens by claiming all schools should adopt four-day weeks, then in the body only defends the idea for primary schools. What should you report as the final claim?
o: Schools should not change at all
All schools should adopt four-day weeks
Primary schools should adopt four-day weeks
ex.why: The body narrows the claim to primary schools, so the refined version is the one the essay actually defends. The opening version is too broad, and the other options are not what the essay argues.

lessons.tip: The claim you should report is the one the essay finally defends.

quiz.q: Why do writers sometimes narrow a claim across an essay?
o: To make it easier to disagree with
To match it to the evidence they actually have
quiz.why: Narrowing lets the writer keep the claim within what the evidence can support.

quiz.q: What is a digression in a long essay?
o: A section that does not relate to the main claim
quiz.why: A digression wanders away from the claim, so it does not directly support or test it.

lessons.t: Judging whether evidence supports a claim
lessons.intro: You will learn what makes something count as evidence for a claim. Knowing this lets you tell real support from decoration in any argument.

cards.b: Evidence is information that can be observed, measured or verified, such as a count, an experiment or a record. It gives a reason to believe the claim beyond the writer's say so. Repeating the claim more often does not count as evidence.
Evidence must bear directly on the claim it supports. A large set of data about one thing does not prove a claim about another. Ask how directly the information connects to the point being made.
Ten careful measurements can be stronger than a thousand careless opinions. Consider how the data were gathered and whether the method was sound. Good evidence is reliable as well as plentiful.

fig.title: Testing evidence
fig.note: Evidence must relate to the claim and come from a reliable source.

ex.q: A writer claims a new bridge reduced accidents. Which is the strongest evidence?
o: Residents say they like the bridge
Accident counts fell after the bridge opened, compared with nearby roads
ex.why: Accident counts measured before and after, compared with a similar area, directly test the claim. The other options are opinions, decoration or unrelated events.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the evidence would look different if the claim were false.

quiz.q: Which best describes evidence?
o: Information that can be checked and bears on the claim
quiz.why: Evidence must be verifiable and directly relevant to the claim it supports.

quiz.q: A claim that a diet works is supported by five people's stories. What is the main weakness?
o: The stories cannot be checked or generalised
quiz.why: Individual stories can be vivid, but they cannot be checked against a wider group and may not be representative.

lessons.t: Anecdotes versus representative data
lessons.intro: You will learn why one vivid story is weaker evidence than data gathered from a representative group. This matters because stories are memorable and easy to believe.

cards.b: A personal story can make a claim feel real, because it gives a face and emotion to the point. However, one story cannot show how common something is. Treat anecdotes as illustrations rather than proof.

Data from a group that reflects the wider population can show how common an effect is. A survey of several hundred people from different areas tells you more than one interview. Check whether the group was chosen fairly.
A survey of only students at one gym may not describe the whole town. Look at who was included and who was left out. A representative group is one that resembles the population the claim is about.

fig.title: Growing the group
fig.note: Larger, fairly chosen groups give firmer evidence.

ex.q: A writer claims most people sleep badly, supported by one friend's story. Which evidence would best support the claim?
o: A photo of a tired friend
A quote from a famous actor
A survey of 2000 people randomly chosen
ex.why: A large, randomly chosen group reflects the population, so it can show how common poor sleep is. The other options are anecdotes or irrelevant to how common the problem is.

lessons.tip: A vivid story tells you what is possible, while data tells you what is typical.

quiz.q: Why are anecdotes persuasive?
quiz.why: Personal stories engage emotion, which makes claims feel convincing even when they prove little.

quiz.q: What makes a group representative?
o: It resembles the population the claim concerns
It is the largest group possible
It is chosen from the writer's friends
quiz.why: A representative group reflects the wider population, so its results can speak to that population.

lessons.t: Group size and how far to trust it
lessons.intro: You will learn how the number of people in a study affects how precisely it measures something. Knowing this helps you judge whether a small study can support a firm claim.

cards.b: With only 20 people, one unusual person can shift the result a lot. Results from small groups can change sharply if the study is repeated. Be cautious about firm claims drawn from them.
As a group grows, its average tends to settle closer to the true value. Doubling the size does not halve the uncertainty, but the gains are real. Larger studies usually support firmer claims.

Many surveys report a margin of error, such as plus or minus three points. If two results differ by less than that margin, the gap may be noise. Use this range to judge whether a difference is meaningful.

fig.title: Margin of error by size
fig.note: Approximate margin of error, in percentage points.

ex.q: A poll of 25 people says 60 percent support a plan, with a margin of error of about 20 points. Which conclusion is best?
o: The true support could be anywhere from about 40 to 80 percent
The poll proves the plan is popular
ex.why: A margin of 20 points around 60 percent gives a range from about 40 to 80 percent. The poll is too imprecise to fix the true value or prove popularity.

lessons.tip: A small group can be interesting but rarely settles a close question.

quiz.q: Why are small groups less reliable?
o: Chance variation can shift results a lot
They are always biased toward the writer
quiz.why: With few people, unusual individuals have a large effect on the average.

quiz.q: A margin of error of 3 points, with results of 51 and 52 percent, means what?
o: The gap is within the uncertainty, so it may be noise
quiz.why: A one-point gap sits well inside a three-point margin, so it cannot be confidently distinguished from chance.

lessons.t: Spotting correlation mistaken for cause
lessons.intro: You will learn why two things moving together does not prove that one causes the other. Spotting this error is one of the most valuable skills in reading arguments.

cards.b: Two variables can rise and fall together without one causing the other. Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer. Shared movement is a clue to investigate, not proof of cause.

A common cause, sometimes called a confounder, can drive both things at once. In the summer example, heat drives both ice cream sales and swimming. Ask whether something else could explain both patterns.

Even when one thing does cause another, the arrow might point the other way. Reading ability and hours of reading may reinforce each other. Consider whether the claim reverses the likely order of events.

fig.title: A hidden common cause
fig.note: A hidden third factor can drive both patterns.

ex.q: A study finds children who own bikes have better grades. The writer claims bikes improve grades. What is the best criticism?
o: The study used a small font
Family support may drive both bikes and grades
ex.why: A third factor such as family support could explain both owning a bike and doing better in school. The writer's causal claim does not follow from the correlation alone.

lessons.tip: When two things move together, ask what else could be moving them both.

quiz.q: What is a confounder?
o: A third factor that can influence both things
quiz.why: A confounder affects both variables, creating a link between them that is not causal.

quiz.q: Which statement shows correlation rather than proven cause?
o: Dropping a glass makes it break every time
Cities with more parks have more cyclists, though the cause is unclear
Water boils at 100 degrees at sea level
quiz.why: The link between parks and cyclists is an association whose direction and cause are not established.

lessons.t: Checking who produced the evidence
lessons.intro: You will learn how to judge whether the people behind evidence are reliable and free of conflicts of interest. A source's background can change how much weight its evidence deserves.

cards.b: Research paid for by a company that sells the product may be shaped by that interest. This does not make it false, but it deserves a closer look. Check whether the funder's interests match the claim.
Look at whether the author has relevant training and published work that others have reviewed. An expert in one field may be less reliable outside it. Credentials help but do not settle the question.

Advocacy groups often publish evidence that supports their cause, which can be useful but selective. Ask whether the source wants to inform you or to win you over. Balanced sources often mention limits and counterpoints.

fig.title: Stronger versus weaker sources
fig.note: Not a verdict, but a useful checklist.

ex.q: A report praising a supplement is funded by the company that sells it. What is the most sensible response?
o: Check the methods and whether independent studies agree
ex.why: Funding creates a potential conflict, so you should test the methods and look for independent confirmation. Accepting or dismissing the report outright would both skip that check.

lessons.tip: Follow the money, then follow the method.

quiz.q: Why does funding matter when judging evidence?
o: It may create an interest that shapes the findings
quiz.why: A funder with a stake in the outcome can influence what is studied or reported, so you should look closer.

quiz.q: What is peer review?
o: Checking by other experts before publication
quiz.why: Peer review means qualified experts assess the work before it is published, which adds a layer of scrutiny.

lessons.t: Does the evidence fit the claim?
lessons.intro: You will learn to check whether evidence actually bears on the claim it is meant to support. Evidence that is accurate but off-topic can still mislead you.

cards.b: A claim about one thing needs evidence about that thing, not a neighbouring one. Data about gym membership cannot prove that exercise improves memory unless memory was measured. Match the question the evidence answers with the question the claim asks.

Writers sometimes cite impressive statistics about a related subject to lend weight to their point. Ask whether the statistic was measured on the same group, time and measure. A true fact can still be irrelevant.
Evidence can be directly relevant yet weak, and irrelevant evidence can look impressive. Judge both questions separately. Ask first whether it fits, then how strong it is.

fig.title: Does the evidence fit?
fig.note: Relevance is checked by asking whether the evidence tests this exact claim.

ex.q: A writer claims a new diet lowers blood pressure, citing a study showing the diet increased energy levels. What is the problem?
o: The evidence measures energy, not blood pressure
ex.why: The study does not measure the outcome named in the claim. Relevance requires that the evidence tests blood pressure, and this evidence does not.

lessons.tip: Write down what the claim predicts, then check that the evidence measures it.

quiz.q: What does relevance mean for evidence?
o: It bears directly on the claim being made
quiz.why: Relevant evidence addresses the same question the claim asks.

quiz.q: A claim that a road is dangerous is supported by data on car sales. Why is this weak?
o: Car sales do not measure road danger
quiz.why: Car sales say nothing about accidents or hazards, so the evidence does not test the claim.

lessons.t: Recognising cherry-picked evidence
lessons.intro: You will learn how to spot evidence that has been selected to favour one side. Cherry-picking can make an ordinary trend look like a strong case, so it is worth detecting early.

cards.b: Cherry-picking means choosing only the results that support a view and ignoring the rest. A writer may quote the best year while skipping weaker ones. Ask what was left out before accepting the selection.

Good evidence usually shows a baseline or a comparison group. If a claim says sales doubled but gives no earlier figure, the comparison is missing. Missing context is often a sign of selective reporting.

Changing the start or end date of a graph can make a trend appear or vanish. Switching between different measures, such as totals and averages, can also mislead. Confirm the period and definition used.

fig.title: Five years, no clear rise
fig.note: Flat over five years, with no clear rise.

ex.q: A report shows only the 2022 sales peak of 101 to claim sales are booming. The full five-year data, shown in the chart, was flat. What is the best description?
o: The chart is cherry-picked and gives a misleading trend
The chart shows the full picture
The data proves a boom every year
ex.why: By showing only one favourable year and hiding the flat trend, the report selects evidence to support a claim the full data does not support. The other options ignore the omitted years.

lessons.tip: Ask what the writer would have shown if the data had gone the other way.

quiz.q: What is cherry-picking in evidence?
o: Selecting only results that support a view
quiz.why: Cherry-picking selects favourable results and ignores the rest, distorting the overall picture.

quiz.q: Why is a missing baseline a warning sign?
o: It shows the data is recent
Without it, you cannot tell whether a change is large
quiz.why: A comparison point shows whether a number has really changed, so its absence makes a claim hard to judge.

lessons.t: Comparing two sources that disagree
lessons.intro: You will learn how to work out why two credible sources reach opposite conclusions. Often the difference lies in definitions, methods or time periods rather than in who is right.

cards.b: Start by stating exactly what each source claims, then identify where they diverge. Sometimes they measure different things with the same name. Narrowing the disagreement shows which question is really in dispute.

Two studies may gather data differently or cover different years and places. A difference in group, period or definition can produce opposite results without either being careless. Note these details before judging.

After finding the cause of disagreement, decide which source has the better method for your question. Sometimes both are partly right, and the truth sits between them. Avoid choosing based only on which conclusion you prefer.

fig.title: Compare the two accounts
fig.note: Lining up the claim and method shows where they differ.

ex.q: Study A says a town's crime fell, using police reports. Study B says it rose, using resident surveys. What is the most likely reason they differ?
o: One of them must have lied
They measured different things with different methods
The towns were not the same
ex.why: Police reports count recorded incidents while surveys capture experiences, and these can move in different directions. That difference explains the disagreement without either source being dishonest.

lessons.tip: When sources clash, first ask whether they are answering the same question.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of two credible sources disagreeing?
quiz.why: Different definitions, groups or periods can lead to opposite results from honest work.

quiz.q: Which approach is best when two sources conflict?
o: Pick the one you like most
Identify the exact point of difference and compare methods
quiz.why: Locating the disagreement and judging the methods is a fair way to decide which evidence is stronger.

lessons.t: When an expert's opinion counts
lessons.intro: You will learn when an expert's opinion counts as useful support and when it is only a claim to be checked. Experts are valuable, but their authority is not the same as proof.

cards.b: A specialist's view is more informed than a random opinion, so it deserves attention. But an expert can be wrong, and their judgement can drift outside their field. Treat the view as a reason to look further.
A strong expert opinion points to data, reasoning or consensus among specialists. A bare assertion from one person is weaker. Ask what the view rests on before giving it much weight.

When many experts in a field independently reach the same conclusion, that agreement is more persuasive than any single voice. Look for consensus statements from recognised bodies. Disagreement among experts is a sign the question is still open.

fig.title: Expert opinion versus evidence

pts: Hard to check on its own

fig.note: An opinion alone is weaker than shown data.

ex.q: A writer says 'a famous physicist believes this diet works' but gives no data. What is the best assessment?
o: The claim has weak support, since the opinion is not based on shown evidence
ex.why: An opinion without shown data is only partial support, and the physicist's view may be outside their field. The claim needs evidence about diets to be persuasive.

lessons.tip: An expert's reasons are worth more than the expert's name.

quiz.q: What makes expert consensus persuasive?
o: Independent specialists reaching the same conclusion
quiz.why: Independent agreement among specialists is stronger than a single voice, since it reduces the chance of one person's error.

quiz.q: Why might an expert's opinion be weak support?
o: It may be outside their field or lack shown reasoning
quiz.why: Expertise is specific, and an opinion without reasons cannot be checked.

lessons.t: Weighing evidence on both sides
lessons.intro: You will learn how to weigh evidence that points in different directions without ignoring either side. Fair weighing protects you from confirming what you already believed.

cards.b: Before deciding, find the best argument against the claim, not a weak caricature of it. Strong counter-evidence deserves the same care you give supporting evidence. Ask what would change your mind.
Six weak studies may be outweighed by two large, well designed ones. Compare reliability, relevance and size rather than tallying supporters. A balance of quality can point clearly in one direction.

Sometimes the evidence genuinely points in mixed directions, and the honest answer is that it is uncertain. A qualified conclusion is more accurate than a confident one. Say which way the balance leans and how sure you are.

fig.title: Studies by result
fig.note: Count both sides, then weigh their quality before judging.

ex.q: Three well designed studies find a drug helps, and two weaker studies find no effect. What is the fairest conclusion?
o: The two weak studies cancel everything
The drug probably helps, with uncertainty, since the stronger studies favour it
ex.why: Weighing by quality, the three stronger studies favour the drug, so it probably helps, though some uncertainty remains. Counting alone or ignoring the weaker studies would both be unfair.

lessons.tip: Ask which side the strongest evidence supports, not which side has more items.

quiz.q: Why should you consider the best counter-argument?
o: To judge the claim against its strongest opposition
To prove the claim is wrong
quiz.why: Testing a claim against its best objections gives a fairer view of how well it stands.

quiz.q: What is a fair way to weigh conflicting studies?
o: Count the number of studies only
Choose the study with the nicest title
Weigh the quality, relevance and size of each
quiz.why: Quality and relevance matter more than raw counts, so the strongest evidence should carry the most weight.

lessons.t: What an inference means in reading
lessons.intro: You will learn what an inference is and why good readers draw conclusions the text does not state directly. This skill helps you understand stories, arguments and instructions more fully.

cards.b: An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know. The writer does not have to state it for it to be supported. Good inferences rest on evidence you can point to.

Stated meaning is what the text says outright, while implied meaning is what it suggests. A character who checks the clock twice may be implied to be anxious. Readers who notice implied meaning understand more than the words alone.

A guess becomes a valid inference only when the text gives you reasons for it. Avoid assuming things that nothing in the passage supports. Always be ready to point to the line that supports your conclusion.

fig.title: Clues build a conclusion
fig.note: Combine the clues to reach what the text implies.

ex.q: A passage says: 'Maya packed her umbrella, checked the forecast twice, and put on her boots.' What can you infer?
o: Maya is going to the beach
ex.why: Packing an umbrella, checking the forecast and wearing boots together suggest she expects rain. The text does not state this, but the clues point clearly to it.

lessons.tip: An inference is a conclusion you can justify with a specific line.

quiz.q: What is an inference?
o: A conclusion drawn from clues and reasoning
quiz.why: An inference joins textual clues with reasoning to reach a conclusion the text may not state.

quiz.q: Which is a valid inference from the sentence 'He left his coat, though the night was freezing'?
o: He is a fan of coats
He may be in a hurry or forgetful
quiz.why: Leaving a coat on a freezing night suggests he may be in a hurry or forgetful, while the other options contradict or go beyond the sentence.

lessons.t: Reading implied meaning in a passage
lessons.intro: You will learn how to find meaning that a passage suggests rather than states. Implied meaning often carries the author's real intent, so it is worth practising.

cards.b: Specific word choices can carry implied meaning, such as calling a plan bold rather than risky. Each word shifts the impression the reader forms. Notice where the author picks vivid or loaded terms.

Sometimes an omission tells you as much as a statement, such as a letter that never mentions a promised refund. Ask what a careful writer would have included if the point were simple. Missing information can imply a lot.

Small concrete details, like a cold cup of tea or an unread letter, often suggest a mood or situation. Gather several details and see what they point to together. A pattern across details is more reliable than a single one.

fig.title: Clues and the implied point
fig.note: The highlighted step is where the reader draws the inference.

ex.q: A passage describes a manager who 'arrived early, reviewed every report, and said little in the meeting.' What is the most likely implied meaning?
o: The manager is thorough and cautious
ex.why: Arriving early and reviewing every report suggest diligence, and saying little suggests caution. Together these clues point to a thorough, careful manager rather than a careless one.

lessons.tip: Gather three details before settling on an implied meaning.

quiz.q: What can an author's word choice imply?
o: Attitude or mood beyond the literal meaning
quiz.why: Loaded or specific words carry connotations that suggest feelings and judgements.

quiz.q: Why can an omission be meaningful?
o: A missing detail can suggest what the writer avoids or doubts
quiz.why: What a careful writer leaves out can suggest avoidance, doubt or a hidden point.

lessons.t: Inferring a writer's attitude or tone
lessons.intro: You will learn how to infer a writer's attitude from tone, meaning the feeling their language conveys. Recognising tone helps you tell whether a writer is praising, mocking or simply informing.

cards.b: Tone describes the attitude a writer takes toward the subject, such as admiration, irritation or amusement. It is conveyed through word choice, sentence rhythm and emphasis rather than stated outright. Name the tone in one word to test your reading.

Words such as truly, absolutely or utterly can signal strong feeling, while exclamation marks suggest energy or emphasis. Irony can reverse the surface meaning, so read carefully. Check whether the words are meant literally.

Irony means saying one thing while meaning another, such as calling a disastrous plan a masterpiece. Context and tone reveal the reversal. Look for mismatches between the praise and the situation described.

fig.title: Reading the tone
fig.note: Name the tone in one word, then test it against the text.

ex.q: A review says: 'The restaurant was truly a masterpiece of patience, since we waited two hours for cold soup.' What is the writer's attitude?
ex.why: Calling a two-hour wait for cold soup a masterpiece of patience is ironic, so the praise is mocking. The tone is sarcastic and disappointed rather than sincerely pleased.

lessons.tip: When praise meets an awful situation, suspect irony.

quiz.q: What does tone describe?
o: The writer's attitude toward the subject
quiz.why: Tone reflects how the writer feels about what they describe.

quiz.q: What signals irony in a sentence?
o: A mismatch between the praise and the context
quiz.why: Irony reverses the surface meaning, so a conflict between the words and the situation signals it.

lessons.t: Filling gaps in an argument
lessons.intro: You will learn how to spot a missing step in an argument and infer what the writer must be assuming. Filling the gap shows whether the reasoning actually holds together.

cards.b: Writers often omit a link that seems obvious, such as the step between a fact and the conclusion. Readers fill the gap automatically, which can hide a weakness. Making the missing step explicit reveals what the argument depends on.

Rewrite the argument with the hidden step added, so you can see the full chain. For example, 'The bus is late, so I will be late' needs the premise that you depend on that bus. A clear premise is easier to test than a vague sense of logic.

Once the premise is visible, ask whether it is true or at least reasonable. If the argument needs a shaky premise, the conclusion is weaker. Good reasoners check the gaps as carefully as the stated points.

fig.title: Bridging the gap
fig.note: The missing link is an unstated assumption joining the premises to the claim.

ex.q: Argument: 'Mia studied all night, so she will pass the exam.' What unstated premise is needed?
o: Studying all night is the only way to pass
ex.why: The conclusion requires a link between the study and the result, and the premise that effective study leads to passing supplies it. The other options are either irrelevant or assume too much.

lessons.tip: Name the hidden step before judging whether the argument works.

quiz.q: What is an unstated premise?
o: A premise the writer states at the end
A hidden assumption that the conclusion depends on
quiz.why: An unstated premise is a required assumption the writer leaves implicit.

quiz.q: Why make a hidden step explicit?
o: To check whether it is true and reasonable
quiz.why: Stating the premise lets you test it, which reveals whether the argument is sound.

lessons.t: Predicting what comes next in a text
lessons.intro: You will learn how to predict what a text is likely to say next by using its structure and earlier clues. Prediction sharpens your attention and tests your understanding as you read.

cards.b: Paragraphs often follow patterns such as problem, evidence, then solution. Recognising the pattern lets you anticipate the next move. When a writer announces three reasons, expect all three to be delivered.
A detail introduced early, such as a locked door or a missed deadline, often returns later. Writers plant clues that shape what follows. Note the setups, then predict how they will be used.
Make a prediction, then read on to test it, adjusting if the text surprises you. Prediction works best as a hypothesis rather than a certainty. Revising your guess is a sign of active reading.

fig.title: Setup predicts the next beat
fig.note: Earlier setup often signals what follows.

ex.q: A passage says: 'Three reasons explain the decline. The first is rising costs.' What should you expect next?
o: The second and third reasons for the decline
ex.why: The writer announced three reasons and gave the first, so the next paragraphs should deliver the second and third. The other options ignore the structure the text sets up.

lessons.tip: Announced lists nearly always get completed.

quiz.q: Why are announced structures useful for prediction?
o: They set expectations that the text usually fulfils
They only appear at the end
quiz.why: When a writer announces a structure, readers can reasonably expect it to be completed.

quiz.q: What is a setup in a text?
o: A detail planted early that may return later
quiz.why: Early details often become important later, so they help you predict what follows.

lessons.t: Inferring motives from actions
lessons.intro: You will learn how to infer why a character or person acts as they do, using the actions described. Motives are rarely stated, so they must be read from the evidence the text provides.

cards.b: People in texts often act in ways that reflect their goals, fears or values. Describing a character who keeps spare keys suggests caution about being locked out. Read each action as a possible window into motive.

The same action can have several motives, so test more than one explanation. A character who gives away money might be generous, guilty or trying to impress. Choose the motive best supported by the surrounding details.
Earlier and later events help confirm or reject a motive. If a character later refuses a loan, a motive of protecting savings becomes more likely. Look for the pattern across the whole text.

fig.title: Action to motive
fig.note: Saving money points to a motive about the future.

ex.q: A passage says: 'Every night, Tom double-checked the stove, even though he had turned it off hours earlier.' What is the most likely motive?
o: He is training for a race
ex.why: Repeatedly checking something already turned off suggests anxiety or a need to feel safe. The other motives do not explain the repeated checking.

lessons.tip: Ask what need the action would satisfy.

quiz.q: What makes a motive well supported?
o: It is the most dramatic one
The surrounding details point to it
The writer names it in the title
It is the first idea you have
quiz.why: Motives should be backed by the evidence in the text, not chosen for drama or speed.

quiz.q: Why test several possible motives?
o: One action can have several explanations
quiz.why: Actions can be driven by different goals, so comparing explanations helps find the best fit.

lessons.t: Reading numbers for unstated conclusions
lessons.intro: You will learn to draw conclusions from numbers that the writer does not state explicitly. Reading figures well means noticing what they imply, and what they cannot tell you.

cards.b: A figure like a 100 percent increase may come from a tiny starting number. Going from 1 customer to 2 is a doubling, but it is small in absolute terms. Ask what the base amount was before judging the size of a change.

An average can be pulled by a few extreme values, so the typical case may differ. A town's mean income may be high even when most residents earn less. Look for the median or the spread when it matters.

Numbers from different groups or periods are only comparable if the measures match. Comparing this year's total with last year's average can produce false conclusions. Check that both sides are measured the same way.

fig.title: Doubling each step
fig.note: A doubling looks large, but the starting base matters.

ex.q: A shop says sales doubled, from 5 to 10 customers a week. What is the most accurate inference?
o: The shop is now very large
Sales rose a lot in percentage terms but from a small base
ex.why: Doubling is a 100 percent rise, but it is from only five customers, so the absolute numbers are small. The other options add claims about size, history or the future that the figures do not support.

lessons.tip: Always ask what the percentage is a percentage of.

quiz.q: Why can a large percentage rise still be a small change?
o: The starting base may be very small
quiz.why: A percentage describes change relative to the starting value, so a small base can inflate the figure.

quiz.q: What can a few extreme values do to an average?
o: Pull it away from the typical value
quiz.why: Extreme values shift the mean, so it may not represent a typical case.

lessons.t: Spotting unstated assumptions
lessons.intro: You will learn how to identify assumptions that a claim depends on but never states. Assumptions are often where arguments quietly succeed or fail.

cards.b: An assumption is something the writer takes for granted, such as that people act rationally or that data are accurate. Claims often rest on several assumptions at once. Identifying them shows what the argument would need to be true.

Phrases like obviously, of course or the real question is often carry hidden assumptions. They signal the writer expects you to agree without proof. Pause at these words and ask what is being taken for granted.
A quick test is to imagine the assumption is false and see whether the claim still holds. If the conclusion collapses, the assumption is doing essential work. Such assumptions deserve close scrutiny.

fig.title: Surfacing an assumption
fig.note: Assumptions often hide inside the wording of a claim.

ex.q: A politician says: 'Obviously, lower taxes will boost growth.' Which assumption is hidden?
o: Lower taxes cause growth rather than merely accompanying it
Taxes are always paid in cash
ex.why: The claim needs the causal assumption that lowering taxes leads to growth. The word obviously signals the writer expects agreement without proof. The other options do not affect the logic.

lessons.tip: Words like obviously often mark an assumption doing quiet work.

quiz.q: What is an assumption in an argument?
o: A belief taken for granted that the claim depends on
quiz.why: Assumptions are background beliefs that the argument needs to be true, but it does not state.

quiz.q: What is a good test for an assumption?
o: Imagine it is false and see if the claim still holds
quiz.why: If the claim collapses without the assumption, the assumption was essential to the argument.

lessons.t: Testing inferences against the text
lessons.intro: You will learn to test whether an inference is actually supported by the text rather than by your own expectations. Checking against evidence keeps your interpretations honest.

cards.b: For each inference, locate a specific sentence or detail that supports it. If you cannot point to any line, the inference is probably your own addition. Quote or paraphrase the evidence to be sure.

Readers often infer what they expect or hope to find, especially on familiar topics. Notice when an inference matches your own beliefs more than the text. Recheck those inferences against the wording.
A tempting inference may conflict with a later detail that corrects it. Good readers revise their conclusion when the text pushes back. Consider the whole passage before finalising a reading.

fig.title: Testing an inference
fig.note: If the cited line could support a different conclusion, the inference needs more work.

ex.q: A passage says the library was 'nearly empty every afternoon'. A reader infers 'the library is failing and should close'. What is the best assessment of this inference?
o: Well supported, since empty libraries should close
Supported, because libraries are always busy
Not supported, since the text reports emptiness but no decline or closure plan
Supported, because the passage mentions afternoons
ex.why: The text reports low use in afternoons but says nothing about decline, funding or closure. The inference adds a conclusion the passage does not provide, so it is not supported.

lessons.tip: If the line you cite could support a different conclusion, your inference needs more work.

quiz.q: What should you do before accepting an inference?
o: Accept it if it sounds right
Find a specific line in the text that supports it
quiz.why: A reliable inference is grounded in textual evidence you can point to.

quiz.q: Why might a reader's inference be biased?
o: They may read what they expect or hope to find
quiz.why: Prior beliefs can make us see support for conclusions the text does not actually provide.

lessons.t: Strong versus weak inferences
lessons.intro: You will learn how to decide whether one inference is stronger than another. Some conclusions follow tightly from the evidence, while others only loosely suggest it.

cards.b: A strong inference is one that the evidence makes likely, with few plausible alternatives. A weak inference could be true but is not clearly required. Ask how many other explanations fit the same clues.

A specific conclusion tied to concrete details is usually easier to support than a sweeping one. Concluding that a person is nervous from trembling hands is more precise than concluding their whole personality. Narrower claims often carry less risk.
A weak inference jumps from a small clue to a large conclusion. One raised eyebrow does not establish a whole plot twist. Notice where the leap happens, and judge the inference accordingly.

fig.title: Strong versus weak inference
fig.note: Strong inferences make fewer leaps.

ex.q: Which inference from 'She checked her watch twice during the meeting' is strongest?
o: She may be anxious about time or wanting to leave
ex.why: Checking a watch repeatedly fits a narrow, plausible reading about time pressure or wanting to leave. The other options leap far beyond a single observed action.

lessons.tip: The fewer leaps an inference makes, the stronger it tends to be.

quiz.q: What makes an inference strong?
o: The evidence makes it likely with few better alternatives
It is the first idea you had
quiz.why: Strength depends on how well the evidence supports the conclusion relative to alternatives.

quiz.q: Which is a weak inference?
o: A specific conclusion with clear support
A cautious reading of the detail
A small clue leading to a huge conclusion
A conclusion matched by several clues
quiz.why: Leaping from one small clue to a sweeping conclusion is what makes an inference weak.

lessons.t: Inferring meaning from context clues
lessons.intro: You will learn how to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word from the sentences around it. Context clues help you understand a passage without stopping to look up every term.

cards.b: The words before and after an unknown term often hint at its meaning. A definition, a contrast or an example may be nearby. Read the whole sentence, then the one before, to gather the clues.

Phrases like in other words, such as, unlike and although signal meaning. In the phrase unlike the clear pond, the lake was turbid, the contrast suggests turbid means cloudy. Use these signals to narrow down the meaning.
Substitute your guessed meaning into the sentence to see whether it still makes sense. If it fits the logic and tone, your guess is probably right. If not, look for other clues.

fig.title: Working out a new word
fig.note: Test the guess by putting it back into the sentence.

ex.q: 'The river was turbid after the storm, unlike the clear water upstream.' What does turbid most likely mean?
ex.why: The word unlike sets turbid against clear, so turbid must describe water that is not clear, meaning cloudy or muddy. The other options describe qualities the sentence does not contrast.

lessons.tip: A word's opposite is often named nearby.

quiz.q: Which signal phrase often introduces a definition or restatement?
quiz.why: In other words restates the meaning of a term in simpler language.

quiz.q: What is a good way to check a guessed meaning?
o: Substitute the guess and see whether the sentence still makes sense
quiz.why: Substitution tests whether the guessed meaning fits the logic and tone of the sentence.

lessons.t: Combining clues to reach a conclusion
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine several clues into one well-supported conclusion. Strong reading rarely depends on a single detail, so this skill ties together everything you have practised.

cards.b: Look for several separate details that point toward the same idea. Clues may be scattered across paragraphs rather than gathered in one place. Make a short list of them before reasoning further.
Some clues are direct and specific, while others are vague or ambiguous. Give more weight to the direct ones and treat weak ones with caution. A conclusion resting on strong clues is more secure.
Write your conclusion in one sentence, followed by the clues that back it. This keeps the reasoning visible and easy to check. If a clue contradicts your conclusion, revise the conclusion.

fig.title: Combining clues
fig.note: Work from separate clues to one supported conclusion.

ex.q: Clues: the cafe sells out of bread by noon, customers queue outside at 8am, and the owner says demand is high. What is the best conclusion?
o: Demand for the bread is high
ex.why: Three separate clues, selling out early, morning queues and the owner's statement, all point to high demand. The other options are not supported by any of the clues.

lessons.tip: A conclusion backed by several independent clues is hard to knock down.

quiz.q: Why combine several clues rather than rely on one?
o: Several independent clues make a conclusion more secure
quiz.why: Independent clues that agree support the conclusion more firmly than any single detail.

quiz.q: What should you do if a clue contradicts your conclusion?
o: Delete the clue from the text
quiz.why: A contradicting clue is evidence against your reading, so the conclusion should be adjusted to fit it.
